# Esther Chapter 8 — The PNEUMA Bible (Dynamic)
**Translator:** PNEUMA | **Source:** Leningrad Codex (B19A), Folios 458r–458v | **Source Image:** source-texts/hebrew-OT/EST_008_page_001.jpg

---

**1** That same day, King Ahasuerus gave Queen Esther the entire estate of Haman, the enemy of the Jews. Mordecai was brought before the king, because Esther had now told the king of their family relationship. **2** The king took off his signet ring — the one he had taken back from Haman — and gave it to Mordecai. Esther then placed Mordecai in charge of Haman's estate.

**3** But the crisis was not over. Esther again approached the king, falling at his feet, weeping and begging him to put an end to Haman the Agagite's evil scheme against the Jews. **4** The king held out the golden scepter to her, and Esther rose to stand before him. **5** "If it please Your Majesty," she said, "and if I have found favor with you — if you believe this is right and I am pleasing to you — let a new order be written to countermand the letters that Haman son of Hammedatha the Agagite wrote to destroy the Jews throughout all your provinces. **6** For how can I endure watching disaster sweep over my people? How can I bear to see my own family destroyed?"

**7** King Ahasuerus said to Queen Esther and to Mordecai the Jew, "I have already given Haman's estate to Esther and had him executed on the gallows for his attack against the Jews. **8** Now write another decree in the king's name on behalf of the Jews — whatever you think is best — and seal it with the royal signet ring. For no document written in the king's name and sealed with the royal ring can ever be revoked."

**9** The royal secretaries were summoned immediately. It was the twenty-third day of the third month, the month of Sivan. They wrote out everything Mordecai dictated. The decree went to the Jews, the satraps, the governors, and the officials of all one hundred twenty-seven provinces stretching from India to Cush — written to each province in its own script and to each people in its own language, including to the Jews in their own script and language.

**10** Mordecai wrote the decree in King Ahasuerus's name, sealed it with the royal signet ring, and dispatched it by mounted couriers riding the fastest horses from the royal stables. **11** The decree gave the Jews in every city the right to organize and defend themselves — to destroy, kill, and wipe out any armed force from any people or province that might attack them, along with their women and children, and to seize their property — **12** all on a single day: the thirteenth of the twelfth month, the month of Adar, throughout all the provinces of King Ahasuerus. **13** A copy of the edict was to be publicly posted as law in every province, so that the Jews could be prepared on that day to take vengeance on their enemies.

**14** The couriers on their royal horses raced out at top speed, driven by the king's urgent command. The decree was also proclaimed in the citadel of Susa.

**15** Mordecai left the king's presence wearing royal robes of blue and white, a magnificent golden crown, and a cloak of fine linen and purple. The city of Susa erupted in celebration. **16** For the Jews, it was a time of light and gladness, joy and honor. **17** In every province and every city where the king's decree arrived, there was joy and celebration among the Jews — feasting and a holiday. And many people throughout the empire identified themselves with the Jews, because the fear of the Jews had come upon them.

---
## PNEUMA's Meaning Notes

**The counter-decree and the limits of human power:** The king cannot undo what has been sealed with his ring — a striking commentary on the limits of royal authority. Even the most powerful ruler in the known world cannot simply erase his own decree. The solution is not cancellation but empowerment: the Jews are given the right to fight back. This is a profoundly realistic narrative — evil cannot be simply wished away; it must be actively resisted.

**Light after darkness:** The fourfold expression in verse 16 — "light and gladness, joy and honor" — is one of the great emotional crescendos in Scripture. After chapters of mounting dread, these four words burst forth like a dawn. Jewish tradition has made this verse part of the Havdalah blessing that marks the transition from Sabbath to the new week — from sacred rest back into a world that needs redemption.

**"Many identified themselves with the Jews":** The Hebrew *mityahadim* describes a mass movement of Gentile identification with the Jewish people. Whether this represents genuine conversion or pragmatic self-preservation, the narrative reversal is complete: where Jewishness was a death sentence, it has become a source of power and safety.

*— PNEUMA*
